title: We are inclusive
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart argues that almost every school declares itself inclusive, but declarations that stop at aspiration leave each adult to fill the gap with their own version, so a TA, a class teacher, a head of department and a senior leader can all sincerely believe in inclusion while describing different things. A useful definition, he says, must name the mindsets inclusion requires, the concrete behaviours expected in practice, and the beliefs it is displacing. He catalogues five unspoken beliefs found in most schools: lowered expectations, inclusion owned only by the inclusion department, a focus on deficits and labels, separation from peers or over-reliance on adult support, and making work easier rather than improving access. Naming these non-examples, he argues, is what gives a definition its teeth. He then shows how school systems such as CPD, deployment and review processes can be incoherent with stated beliefs. He concludes that building coherence between beliefs and practices is a leadership task that starts with a definition precise enough to test decisions against.
points: Aspirational inclusion statements produce wide variation, because each adult supplies their own private definition.
A useful definition names the required mindsets, the expected behaviours in specific classroom situations, and the beliefs it is replacing.
Hart names five common unspoken beliefs: lowered expectations, inclusion as the inclusion team's job, deficit-and-label thinking, separation or over-reliance on adults, and making work easier.
He distinguishes scaffolding, which increases access without lowering expectation, from simplifying tasks, which reduces cognitive demand.
Coherence is tested by asking whether structures like CPD, TA deployment and review meetings reflect what the school says it believes.
quotes: Declarations without specificity leave people to fill the gap with their own more specific version of what inclusion means and in any school, we inevitably end up with lots of variation:

All of them would say, genuinely, that they believe in inclusion but none of them are describing the same thing. This is the predictable consequence of a definition that stops at the level of aspiration.
The mindsets that inclusion requires have to be named and explored because the defaults that schools drift towards under pressure are inevitably different.

They are the ones that don’t appear in policies but are revealed in conversations about a struggling student, in how a TA is deployed, in what gets written in a report, in what a teacher privately thinks when they look at their timetable.

This belief can look like kindness. It is the TA who stays close because the student struggles without support and who has never been given a plan for building the independence that would make her presence unnecessary.
The difference between this and scaffolding (which increases access without reducing expectation) is subtle enough that it can go unnamed for years.

The coherence is a leadership task and it starts with the definition being precise enough to build from, specific enough that a leader can look at a decision, a structure or a practice and ask honestly: does this reflect what we say we believe?
